title: Where International Teachers Save Most in East Asia (China, Vietnam, Korea) 2026
excerpt: A numbers-first comparison of monthly savings for international school teachers in China, Vietnam and South Korea in 2026, including what housing and tax really do to your take-home.
content:
Where International Teachers Save Most in East Asia (China, Vietnam, Korea) 2026

If you're picking between China, Vietnam and South Korea because you want to leave with money in the bank, the headline savings figures make it look like a photo finish. It isn't. Once you strip out housing, tax and the cost-of-living gap, the three markets sit at genuinely different price points and the ordering flips depending on which tier of school hires you. Here's the 2026 picture with the numbers verified, and where the traps are hiding.

The headline numbers

Salaries and savings estimates for teachers with a state licence or PGCE and 2-5 years of experience, at reputable international schools (not language centres):

CountryMonthly salary (USD)HousingTypical monthly savingsAnnual savings range
Vietnam$2,000–$4,000 [1]Allowance $1,200–$1,800/mo at top schools, or included [1]$500–$1,500 [1][2]$6,000–$18,000
China (Tier 1: Shanghai, Beijing)$2,500–$4,700+; Shanghai international schools 30,000–45,000 RMB ($4,110–$6,165) [3][4]Included or 2,000–4,000 RMB allowance [5]$1,000–$2,000 [4]$12,000–$24,000
China (Tier 2/3)$2,000–$3,500 [3][4]Usually included [4]$1,500–$2,500 [4]$18,000–$30,000
South Korea$2,000–$4,500 (KRW 2,700,000–6,000,000) [6][7]Usually provided or allowance [6]$1,000–$2,500 [7][8]$12,000–$30,000

Two things jump out. First, Korea and China tier-2/3 out-save the more famous tier-1 China packages once you account for how much cheaper the smaller cities are. Second, Vietnam's floor is real. Its ceiling is lower than the other two and only reaches the same annual savings if you land at one of the top HCMC or Hanoi schools with a full package.

The rest of this piece explains why.

Vietnam: the middle ground

Vietnam has become the East Asia entry point most veteran teachers now recommend for a first international post, and the money is a big part of that. Cost of living runs 50-70% below Western standards according to Vietnam Teaching Jobs' 2026 country data [1], and the international school sector has grown fast enough that experienced hires are commanding proper packages rather than the old "backpacker teacher" pay.

At an established international school in Ho Chi Minh City or Hanoi in 2026, expect $2,000-$4,000 a month base [1][9], plus:

  • Housing allowance of $1,200-$1,800/month, or a school-owned apartment
  • Return flights (usually two a year)
  • International health insurance
  • Tuition waivers for up to two dependent children
  • End-of-contract bonus (variable)

Savings from that setup run $500-$1,500/month, depending on whether you eat where the expats eat or where your Vietnamese colleagues do [1][2]. A teacher paid $2,300/month with housing covered, spending $600 on food and transport and another $400 on lifestyle, banks about $1,300/month. Over a two-year contract with modest raises, that's $30,000-plus before flights and bonus.

The specific catch in Vietnam: the "international school" label is doing a lot of work. Genuinely international schools (British, IB, American curriculum) pay the numbers above. "Bilingual" and "international standard" schools pay 30-50% less and skip most of the benefits. If the ad quotes total compensation as one number without breaking out housing, ask for the breakdown before you fly out.

Secondary cities (Da Nang, Nha Trang, Vung Tau) sit 15-25% below HCMC and Hanoi on salary [9] but not proportionally below on cost. Savings work out roughly similar if you're single. Different picture with a family.

China: still the highest absolute savings, if you land right

China's international school sector rebounded after the post-COVID exodus, and by 2026 the salary picture at established schools is genuinely competitive. Shanghai's tier-1 international schools pay 30,000-45,000 RMB per month, which converts to roughly $4,110-$6,165 at current rates [3]. Beijing sits in the same band. Guangzhou and Shenzhen a bit below.

That's the top of the market. Broader ranges cited by Premier TEFL and Moreland for licensed international school teachers in China put the 2026 spread at $2,500-$4,700+ per month across cities and school tiers [4][10]. Almost all include housing (or a 2,000-4,000 RMB monthly allowance), medical, flights, and a completion bonus [5][10]. Some schools also cover children's tuition at their own campus, which is worth $20,000-$40,000 per child per year at tier-1 fees.

Savings potential:

  • Tier-1 cities (Shanghai, Beijing) with housing provided: teachers report saving 40-55% of net take-home, which lands at $1,000-$2,000/month for most [4]
  • Tier-2 and tier-3 cities (Chengdu, Suzhou, Xiamen, Kunming): $1,500-$2,500/month is common because cost of living drops faster than salary [4]

The counter-intuitive result: teachers at mid-tier schools in tier-2 cities often bank more per year than colleagues on higher headline salaries in Shanghai. Someone at $3,500 in Chengdu with school housing can save $2,200/month; someone at $5,000 in Shanghai renting in a decent expat area saves $1,600 after rent, food and the tier-1 lifestyle creep.

The catches in China for 2026:

  • Tax. China taxes worldwide income for anyone resident 183+ days. Rates are progressive; the top of the international school band lands in the 25-30% marginal bracket. Your salary is quoted gross. The tax-free housing/meal allowance concession was extended to end of 2027, which matters because it typically knocks 10-15% off your effective rate if your school structures the package correctly [11].
  • Visa reality. The Z visa still requires a bachelor's minimum, a 120-hour TEFL or equivalent, a state teaching licence for real international school posts, and a clean criminal record. Age cap is 60 in most provinces, 55 in some [11][12]. Processing tightened again in early 2026.
  • Contract structure. Most contracts are two-year, and the completion bonus (typically one month's salary) is only paid if you finish. Leaving mid-contract costs the bonus and often triggers repayment of relocation costs.

For our full read on the China tier-1 market see China's International School Rebound: Teaching in Tier-1 Cities 2026.

South Korea: the highest ceiling for licensed teachers

South Korea's international school segment is smaller than China's and narrower than Vietnam's, but for a licensed subject specialist willing to commit for two or three years, it produces the biggest annual savings figures of the three.

Salaries at genuine international schools (SFS, SIS, KIS, YISS, Chadwick, Dulwich Seoul, GSIS Busan) run KRW 2,700,000-6,000,000/month, which is $2,000-$4,500 [6]. Housing is usually provided or paid via a monthly allowance. Medical is fully covered. Airfare and shipping are covered on entry and exit. Most schools contribute to a severance equal to one month's salary per year of service, paid at the end.

Reported savings by band (from OK Recruiting's 2026 breakdown and The TEFL Academy's Korea savings analysis):

  • Entry-level (Seoul, $38,000-$45,000): save $12,000-$18,000/year [8]
  • Mid-career ($45,000-$55,000): save $18,000-$24,000/year [7][8]
  • Senior ($55,000-$70,000): save $24,000-$30,000/year, sometimes more [7]

Korea's structural advantage is low income tax at the middle of the band. Most licensed teachers pay 5-15% effective income tax after deductions, well below China's 20-25% and roughly matched to Vietnam. Korea's structural disadvantage is cost of living in Seoul. Groceries, dining out and childcare all sit closer to Tokyo than to Bangkok, and lifestyle creep is real. A teacher who eats out three times a week and drinks weekends in Itaewon saves a lot less than the headline figure suggests.

Two Korea-specific things worth pricing in:

  • The severance is real money. One month per year of service, paid tax-favourably at exit. Over three years that's an additional $10,000-$15,000 you don't see in the monthly numbers.
  • Peninsula-only visa. The E-2 (for English teachers) and E-7 (for licensed subject specialists at international schools) tie you to one employer. Changing schools mid-contract is possible but bureaucratic and often costs you time out of country.

The comparison that actually matters

If you optimise for maximum annual savings and you have a state licence plus 5+ years' experience, the ranking in 2026 is:

1. South Korea, senior band ($24,000-$30,000+)

2. China, tier-2/3 cities with housing included ($18,000-$30,000)

3. China, tier-1 cities ($12,000-$24,000)

4. Korea, entry/mid ($12,000-$24,000)

5. Vietnam, top HCMC/Hanoi schools ($12,000-$18,000)

6. Vietnam, mid-market or secondary cities ($6,000-$15,000)

If you optimise for lifestyle plus reasonable savings and you're earlier in your career, Vietnam moves up. Cost of living is genuinely lower, tax is simple, and $800-$1,200/month in savings on a $2,300 salary in HCMC feels different from $1,600 saved on $5,000 in Shanghai where a night out costs three times as much.

If you optimise for total package including dependent tuition, China at tier-1 wins by a distance, because a family with two kids at a $30,000+ per year school effectively adds $60,000/year to compensation.

Reality checks before you sign

Same three checks apply everywhere, worth pricing in explicitly:

  • Get the offer in writing with every line itemised. Base, housing, allowances, insurance, flights, shipping, tuition, bonus, severance, tax withholding responsibility. Verbal "we cover housing" is not a contract.
  • Ask how many teachers renewed for a second contract last year. A school renewing 70%+ tells you the package works in practice. A school renewing 40% is losing people mid-contract for reasons the ad won't mention.
  • Verify the school's international accreditation. CIS, NEASC, WASC or IBO. If it accredits with none of them and calls itself international, it isn't in the sense the salary figures above assume.

For the pre-signing due diligence framework see Why Teachers Break International School Contracts.

Key Takeaways

  • Highest annual savings, 2026: South Korea at senior band ($24,000-$30,000+) and China at tier-2/3 with housing ($18,000-$30,000). Vietnam tops out around $18,000 [4][7].
  • Best entry-level value: Vietnam. Lower ceiling, but lower tax and cost of living mean $500-$1,500/month savings on a first-post salary feel real [1][2].
  • The housing question decides everything. In China and Korea, housing included shifts savings by $10,000-$25,000 a year [9]. In Vietnam, the housing allowance is usually cash, which shifts control back to you but taxes it.
  • Tier-2 China beats tier-1 China on savings for teachers who aren't drawn to Shanghai/Beijing lifestyle. $1,500-$2,500/month against $1,000-$2,000/month [4].
  • Tax matters more than most listings admit. Vietnam and Korea both sit around 5-15% effective for teachers. China lands at 20-25% at the top of the band, though the housing-allowance concession (extended through 2027) softens that [11].

Practical next step: if you're choosing between two offers this recruitment cycle, work the numbers on a per-year basis, not per-month. Bonus, severance, flights and tuition all sit outside monthly pay and they move the ranking by tens of thousands. The offer with the higher monthly headline isn't always the one that pays you more over two years.
